title: What a prophet is
hook: one who speaks for God, usually uncomfortably, to their own people

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block close on the prayer book, and your line was pray what you feel. Which psalm did you choose to keep? Day four hundred sixty-two.

A king has done something terrible. He took another man's wife, and when she became pregnant, he arranged for her husband to die in battle. It's covered up. Nobody at court will say a word. Then a man named Nathan asks for an audience and tells the king a story: a rich man with huge flocks steals a poor man's only lamb, a lamb the poor man's children loved, to serve to a guest. The king is furious. That man deserves to die, he says. And Nathan looks at King David and says four words, in the King James Bible: "Thou art the man." Today, a new block of the path: the prophets. And the first question: what is a prophet?
screen: `A KING'S COVER-UP.` → `A STORY ABOUT A STOLEN LAMB.` → `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: In everyday speech, a prophet is someone who predicts the future. In the Bible, that's a small part of it. The Greek word prophetes means one who speaks for, or speaks forth: a spokesperson. The Hebrew is navi, and some scholars think it means one who is called, or one who calls out. Either way, the job is less fortune-telling than forth-telling: saying what God sees, now, out loud. Now notice who they spoke to. The prophets mostly spoke to their own people. Not to enemies. To their own kings, their own priests, their own neighbors, about their own injustice: the poor cheated in the market, widows ignored, worship that was all show. It was rarely welcome. Jeremiah was beaten and thrown in a pit. Amos was told to go home. Some weren't professionals at all. Amos said he was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but a herdsman and a tender of fig trees. Ordinary people, called to say an uncomfortable thing. And they weren't only stern. The same voices that warned also comforted: Isaiah, whom we meet tomorrow, will speak of swords beaten into plowshares, and of a God who will not forget his people even if a mother could forget her child. In Christian Bibles, the prophets come at the end of the Old Testament: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel, called the major prophets because their books are long, with Lamentations beside Jeremiah, then twelve shorter ones. Jewish Bibles arrange them differently, and count books like Joshua and Kings among the prophets too. In Matthew's Gospel the crowds call Jesus a prophet, and he says, "A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house." Christians honor him as more than a prophet, but they also see him standing in this line.
screen: `NOT FORETELLING: FORTH-TELLING.` · `TO THEIR OWN PEOPLE.` · `A HERDSMAN, NOT A PROFESSIONAL.` · `MAJOR MEANS LONG, NOT IMPORTANT.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one uncomfortable truth. Settle, and breathe. Think of something someone has told you recently that stung: a criticism from a friend, a complaint from your partner, a hard word from a boss, a line in the news that pointed straight at people like you. Notice your first reaction, the defense forming. Set it aside for a moment. Ask honestly: is there any truth in it? Not all of it. Just any. Hold that piece without arguing. If you pray, you can ask for ears to hear it. The bell holds the time.
Prophet. Navi in Hebrew, prophetes in Greek: one called to speak for God, usually uncomfortably, and usually to their own people.
Your line: truth to power. Today, when someone tells you something you don't want to hear, listen all the way to the end before you answer. Day four hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Christians read the prophets throughout the church year, especially in Advent and Lent, and many churches see the prophets' call for justice as part of their own work with the poor; Jewish communities read a passage from the Prophets, the haftarah, every Sabbath.

what it means: someone called to speak for God, usually an uncomfortable word, usually to their own people.

what a scholar hears: navi likely from a root meaning to call. the Greek prophetes is a spokesperson. and in the Hebrew Bible the Prophets include Joshua through Kings, while Daniel sits among the Writings.

notes: Editor pass (y2 review): cut 'most people today think' and 'many weren't professionals'; navi's meaning attributed to 'some scholars'; Lamentations no longer listed as a 'major prophet because its book is long'; the crowds calling Jesus a prophet now cited (Matthew 21:11, added to sources).
Etymology of navi: commonly linked to Akkadian nabu, 'to call'; whether passive ('one called') or active ('one who calls') is debated. Stated as 'scholars think'. Confirm.
'Jeremiah was beaten and thrown in a pit' (Jeremiah 20:2 put in the stocks after being struck; 38:6 cast into a dungeon/cistern). Confirm.
Amos 7:14 paraphrased ('herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit' in KJV). Confirm 'a tender of fig trees' (sycomore-figs).
Christian vs Jewish ordering of the prophets described without ranking. Confirm.
'Christians honor him as more than a prophet' — stated as a Christian belief. Confirm phrasing.

Review pass: Isaiah 49:15 previously summarized as 'a mother who could never forget her child', which inverts the verse (a mother may forget; God will not). Rewritten to match. Also: 'Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel and Daniel, called the major prophets because their books are long' — Lamentations is short and is grouped with Jeremiah by tradition; confirm phrasing.
